title: A boy of twelve
hook: Maha Singh dies and his twelve-year-old son Ranjit Singh inherits the Sukerchakia misl

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rani Sada Kaur, the widow who led the Kanhaiya misl and turned a feud into an alliance. Your line was she backed him. Which young person did you put something behind? Today, the boy she backed. Day nine hundred five.

The chief of the Sukerchakia misl is out on campaign, Sikh histories say, besieging a fort, when he falls ill. He doesn't recover. Maha Singh is dead, and the band he and his father built has no grown man to lead it. What it has is his son. Ranjit. A boy, twelve years old in the usual telling, who until that day has been somebody's child. Now the riders are looking at him. Today: a boy of twelve.
screen: `MAHA SINGH FALLS ILL ON CAMPAIGN.` → `THE CHIEF IS DEAD.` → `THE RIDERS LOOK AT RANJIT.`

segments.voice: Start with how a misl passed from hand to hand. A misl was a band of equals around a chief, and the chief's place could pass to his son. That kept the band together. It also meant that sometimes the son was very young. The riders didn't get to pick a seasoned commander. They got the boy they had. So the first thing to see here is the weight. A boy who should be learning to ride well is suddenly the name on the banner. Every rival chief nearby notices. Some see an opening. Second, notice that Sikh memory already held stories of the very young carrying great weight. Guru Har Krishan became Guru as a small child, and Sikhs remember him for compassion, tending the sick in Delhi. The Guru's younger sons, the Sahibzade, stood firm at Sirhind when they were children. Ranjit is not a Guru and not a martyr. But the people around him had been raised on the idea that age is not the measure of a person. Third, a boy of twelve doesn't lead alone. Sikh histories say others helped hold the reins at first: his mother, his father's trusted men, and the family he was promised into. That help is a story for a few days from now. For today, notice how the young chief begins: with grief, with a band waiting for orders, and with a name he hasn't grown into yet. The histories tell what he grew into. That comes soon. But every one of those later chapters starts here, with a boy standing where his father used to stand. Twelve, and leading.
screen: `THE CHIEF'S PLACE PASSES TO HIS SON.` · `THE WEIGHT ON A BOY.` · `AGE IS NOT THE MEASURE.` · `HE DOESN'T LEAD ALONE.` · then, large: `TWELVE, AND LEADING.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for a young person carrying too much. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone young who has had to grow up fast: a kid looking after younger siblings, a teenager working to help at home, a young adult who lost a parent, maybe the person you once were. Hold them in mind. What would it have meant, or what would it mean now, to hear one sentence of encouragement from an older person? Find that sentence. Keep it simple. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Ranjit, a boy of twelve in the usual telling, whose father Maha Singh died and left him the Sukerchakia misl to lead. Today's word.
Your line: twelve, and leading. Today, encourage one young person who's carrying something heavy. Say the sentence you found. Day nine hundred five.

howItsDone: Sikh histories tell of Maha Singh's death and the young Ranjit Singh inheriting the Sukerchakia misl, the start of the story Sikhs remember as the rise of the Maharaja.

what it means: a boy left chief of one misl among several, after his father died on campaign.
what a scholar hears: leadership in a misl could pass within the chief's family, so a young heir could inherit a band of seasoned riders, and lean on regents at first.

notes: Ranjit's age of twelve comes from the index and is framed in the voice as 'in the usual telling'; confirm (some sources give a slightly different age).
Maha Singh falling ill during a siege (commonly given as Sodhra): framed as 'Sikh histories say'; confirm.
Regency of his mother Raj Kaur, the diwan Lakhpat Rai and Sada Kaur: given only generally ('his mother, his father's trusted men, and the family he had married into'); day 908 tells it. Confirm.

Guru Har Krishan 'became Guru as a small child' and tended the sick in Delhi; the Sahibzade 'stood firm at Sirhind when they were children': no ages given. The voice says Ranjit is not a Guru and not a martyr, to avoid equating them; confirm the Keeper is comfortable with the comparison.
Smallpox and Gujranwala left for day 907.
Editor: Ranjit was betrothed, not yet married, when Maha Singh died; 'the family he had married into' changed to 'the family he was promised into'.
